newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE euroyen firmer on weak stocks, EPA report.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE euroyen firmer on weak stocks, EPA report.

text.p: The key March three-month euroyen futures contract was firmer by midday on Tuesday due to a weakness in share prices and a cautious undertone in the Economic Planning Agency's monthly economic report.
"The EPA's assessment of the economy in its monthly report seemed somewhat cautious, and helped support euroyen futures," a city bank trader said.
But the March seemed to lack the energy for a rise above 99.20, and was likely to be stuck in a range from 99.16 to 99.19 during the day, he said.
The March stood at 99.18 by midday, up from the previous day's settlement of 99.16. Turnover was 26,382 contracts.
Under current market conditions, a near-term fall below 99.15 is unlikely, a trader for a long-term credit bank said.
Unless monetary authorities say something to curb the current declining trend of interest rates, the March is unlikely to stage a sharp fall, the second trader said.
The Bank of Japan drained a net 500 billion yen from the money market in the morning, against a projected fund surplus of 680 billion yen. The market had been expecting a drainage of 400 billion yen.
The operation left the market with a fund surplus of 180 billion yen, down from a surplus of 280 billion yen on Monday.
Traders said the BOJ's decision to reduce the fund surplus in the market, and demand for short-end funds was kept the key overnight call rate stuck near 0.50 percent in the morning.

No new key three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued in the morning. They were offered at 0.62 percent. About 90 billion yen worth of two-month CDs were issued at 0.63 percent. One-month CDs were offered at 0.55 percent.
"It was basically trapped in a three-tick range during the session," said a trader at a European bank.

He said perceptions that a U.S. investment bank was cutting its Japanese stock holdings as part of a cutback in its operations in Japan were partly responsible for weakening Tokyo stock prices and helped firm the Euroyen contract.

The market was also betting that interest rates in Japan would be kept low in light of recent weak economic data, he added. "However, there isn't good reason to buy the euroyen contract further unless there is fresh economic data that points to a slowing down in the economy," he added.

The 225-share Nikkei average shed 153.62 points, or 0.78 percent, to end at 19,514.45. The key 182nd Japanese government bond yield stood at 2.110 percent at 0703 GMT, up from earlier lows of 2.075 percent.

A senior government official said the Japanese government bond market is a bit too pessimistic about Japan's economic outlook, a comment that made some traders wary of buying the euroyen contract. The source said: "It's not a situation that the downside risk for the economy is on the horizon."
The source added: "Ruling out the possibility of an interest rate rise within this year is a bit premature."
